speaker: Derek Lowe
title: Derek Lowe, PhD: A Medicinal Chemist’s Thoughts on Drug Discovery and the Future of Pharma
question: In scientific publishing, what structural incentives have made the academic journal ecosystem feel increasingly broken?
guest: There are too damn many of them. Because of H-indices and citation counts, publications have become the academic currency for promotions. The prestigious journals know that they're prestigious and know the power they wield, and everyone else knows it too—so they charge appropriately for that power. We're in a nasty vicious spiral where journals charge a lot of money, and people feel they have no choice but to pay it because that's how they advance their careers. Then more people start journals because everyone is trying to publish all the time, which brings on a bunch of sleazy, totally dishonest stuff at the low end—so-called open access journals. There are very good open access journals, but you have to pay to publish in them through page and article charges because they don't make money by subscription. A bunch of con artists looked at that and said, 'Why don't we charge people to publish every single thing they send us and not spend any money evaluating it?' You can send random words to some of these outlets, and as long as your check clears, they will publish it. Scientific publishing is unsustainable as it stands.

points.core: Journal publications serve as the mandatory career currency for academic promotions.

points.note: Accept: fraudulent or low-end journals maximizing volume by accepting gibberish or unreviewed papers as long as payment clears. Do not credit: vague complaints about declining paper quality without the pay-to-publish incentive.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core problem is that the people who produce, evaluate, and pay for research are rewarded for things other than reliable science.

Researchers are hired, promoted, and funded largely on publication counts and journal prestige ("publish or perish"), so the rational strategy is to publish often, slice findings thinly, and chase novel, positive results. That feeds publication bias, p-hacking, and the replication crisis, since null results and replications earn little credit.

Publishers, meanwhile, profit from free labor: academics write and peer-review without pay, then institutions buy the work back through costly subscriptions, sustaining profit margins of around 30–40% for the largest commercial houses. The shift to open access fixed the paywall but introduced article processing charges, which pay publishers per accepted paper. That rewards volume over rigor, fueling mega-journals, endless special issues, predatory journals, and paper mills.

Peer review is strained as submissions outgrow the pool of unpaid, uncredited reviewers, making reviews slower and shallower. Metrics such as impact factor and h-index have become targets, inviting citation cartels and gaming. Corrections and retractions remain slow, because nobody is rewarded for them.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: At the heart of scientific publishing’s dysfunction is a misalignment between the pursuit of reliable knowledge and the incentives governing academic careers and publisher profits. Universities and funders tie hiring, tenure, and grants to publication counts, citations, and journal impact factors. This “publish or perish” pressure rewards novel, statistically significant claims over replications, null results, and methodological rigor, fueling questionable research practices, salami-sliced studies, and fraudulent paper mills. Meanwhile, major commercial publishers capture publicly funded research and free academic labor to extract extraordinary profit margins. While traditional subscription paywalls restrict access, the shift toward author-paid open-access fees creates a perverse volume incentive, tempting predatory outlets and established presses alike to expand “special issues” and accept more papers to maximize revenue. Finally, quality control depends on unpaid peer reviewers who receive virtually no institutional credit for careful vetting, producing severe reviewer fatigue, slow turnaround times, and uneven scrutiny as global submissions surge. Together, metric-driven careerism, volume-hungry business models, and unrewarded gatekeeping optimize the ecosystem for quantity and prestige rather than scientific truth.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The core problem is that academic publishing's incentives reward volume and prestige, not reliable knowledge. Hiring, tenure and grant committees lean on publication counts and journal impact factors, so researchers "publish or perish." That favors many small, flashy, positive results over replications, null findings or slow careful work.

Commercial publishers such as Elsevier, Springer Nature and Wiley make profit margins often above 30%. They do it with content and peer review that academics supply for free, then sell back through expensive subscriptions. The shift to open access often just moved the cost to authors. Article processing charges can run over $10,000 at top journals, which rewards publishing more papers. The clearest example is "mega-journals" whose output and special issues ballooned, leading some to lose their index listings.

Paper mills, citation cartels, predatory journals and now AI-generated submissions exploit these metrics. Retractions are reaching record numbers. Meanwhile unpaid reviewers are burning out under ever more submissions, so review quality and speed suffer.

The result is a system where career, profit and prestige incentives all push toward quantity over trustworthiness.

Researchers face intense "publish or perish" pressure, where hiring, tenure, and grants depend heavily on publication counts and journal prestige metrics like the Impact Factor rather than methodological rigor or replicability. Because prestigious journals prioritize novel, eye-catching results, scientists are discouraged from conducting replication studies or publishing null findings, while subtly nudged toward selective reporting and inflated claims. Meanwhile, commercial publishers extract substantial profits from a system reliant on publicly funded research and unpaid academic labor for writing, editing, and peer review. As submission volumes explode, the pool of unpaid peer reviewers is overwhelmed, slowing publication and weakening quality control. Together, these forces reward prestige and quantity over reliable, cumulative science.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Hiring, tenure, and grant decisions often reward publication counts and the prestige of the journals researchers publish in. That makes it rational to split findings into several papers, chase fashionable topics, and emphasize striking results. Journals competing for attention and citations tend to favor novelty and positive findings, so replications, null results, and corrections are harder to publish. The prestige attached to selective journals also encourages researchers to submit the same paper to several journals in succession, adding delays and repeated rounds of review.

The economics reinforce those pressures. Universities and funders pay researchers to do the work, and academics typically review manuscripts without pay. Publishers can then charge libraries for access or charge authors to make articles open access. Libraries have limited leverage because readers need particular articles, while authors need the career credit attached to particular journals. At the same time, where revenue depends on per-article fees, accepting more papers can bring in more money. Together, these incentives reward publication volume, prestige, and revenue more directly than they reward reliable findings, accessible research, or careful peer review.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Researchers need publications in prestigious journals to win jobs, promotions, and grants. When committees use journal reputation and citation counts as shortcuts for judging quality, researchers have strong reasons to publish frequently and pursue striking results. Journals seeking attention also favor novelty, which makes replications, null results, and careful verification harder to publish and less rewarding to pursue.

The economics reinforce those pressures. Researchers supply articles and usually review them without payment from publishers, while libraries buy access and authors or funders may pay publication fees. A library cannot substitute a cheaper journal for a specific paper its readers need, and an author cannot easily substitute a less prestigious venue when a hiring decision is at stake. That gives established publishers pricing power. Where publishers earn a fee for each accepted article, higher volume can also increase revenue. The result is a system in which choices that make sense for individual researchers, journals, and universities can collectively undermine affordability and reliability.
